editorial:
Imagine your whole world falling apart in a second, and instead of dealing with it, you just hide in your room. That is exactly what you get with this story. You follow Wilson, a guy who is totally lost after his wife, Liza, kills herself for reasons he cannot understand. He spends his days huffing gas and playing with remote-controlled cars just to numb the pain. It is a weird, sad, but sometimes funny look at how people break down. You will feel for him, but you will also probably want to shake him and tell him to get his life together, especially while his mother-in-law keeps pushing his buttons.

The acting feels very real, and the slow pace makes you feel the same boredom and sadness that Wilson feels. While it might be too slow for some of you, it hits hard if you like character studies. If you want to check it out, I suggest renting it on Apple TV for a quick watch, or you could add the Blu-ray to your physical collection if you love these kinds of indie gems. It is a quiet movie, so make sure you have a cozy spot and no distractions when you press play.
endingExplained: By the end, you see Wilson finally stop hiding from the truth. He stops the drug use and stops using his games to escape. He has a final, honest talk with his mother-in-law, which helps them both start to heal. He realizes that he cannot find an answer to why Liza left, but he can still choose to live. He finally steps outside and accepts his grief, showing he is ready to move forward.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves quiet stories about grief and recovery.
